chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Hadid, from Murazim, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) entered the house of Mu'ttab one day while he was preparing for the Umrah. He picked up a wooden tablet on which was written a list specifying the provisions for the dependents and what was allocated for them. He found that it listed for So-and-so, and So-and-so, and So-and-so, but there was no exception (condition) mentioned in it. So he said, 'Whoever wrote this book and did not include an exception in it, how does he think it will be fulfilled?' Then he called for the inkwell and said, 'Add to it: If God wills.' So he added 'If God wills' to every name.

key_terms.اسْتِثْنَاءٌ: Exception (specifically the condition of divine will)

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of adding 'If God wills' to lists of provisions or intentions in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) corrects a practical error in recording provisions by adding 'insha'Allah' to each entry, illustrating the Shia scholarly emphasis on distinguishing between absolute divine decree and conditional human expectation. This practice safeguards against *ghurur* (self-deception) regarding future events, reinforcing the theological principle that all worldly affairs are contingent upon God's will, a concept deeply rooted in the verse 'And you do not will except that Allah wills'.
